reading.body:
Kentucky's 2026 legislative session produced six separate bills on data centers, more than on any other AI-adjacent subject.

The pattern is narrow but real. Data centers appear as HB593, HB856, SB319, SB330, and HB544, plus HB314 and SB64 touching the Kentucky Communications Network Authority. Alongside those sit four data privacy bills (HB692, HB633, HB559, HB33), one bill on artificial intelligence itself (HB455), one on mental health chatbots (HB641), one on algorithmic rent-setting (HB201), and one on addictive online platforms (HB227). The rest of the 87 bills are tax credits, licensure compacts, appropriations, and regulated substances, which is to say the ordinary business of a legislature.

For AI specifically, the volume is concentrated where physical infrastructure meets state law. Data centers draw power and water and pay property taxes, so they arrive at the legislature as siting, incentive, and utility questions rather than as technology questions. That is consistent with the idea that compute is downstream of buildings and power, but the data here only shows that legislators filed bills. It does not show what any of them would do, whether they passed, or what a data center in Kentucky consumes.

What this does not tell the reader is outcome. Bill titles and filing dates are not law, and a bill introduced is not a bill enacted. The single news item, on jobs AI cannot easily replace in Indiana and Kentucky, is dated September 2026 and stands alone. Nothing here measures Kentucky's grid capacity, its existing data center load, or the size of any AI operation in the state.

Six data center bills in one session is not six independent proposals. It is one subject arriving through multiple sponsors and multiple chambers at once, which is what happens when a legislature has not yet decided which committee owns a question. HB593, HB856, HB544, SB319, and SB330 all carry the identical title, "AN ACT relating to data centers," and the two Communications Network Authority bills, HB314 and SB64, sit adjacent to them. The titles are placeholders that say a bill exists without saying what it does.

The filing dates cluster in a way the subject matter does not. Four of the five data center bills were filed between February 2 and March 4, 2026, and the two network authority bills landed January 11 and March 9. The privacy bills spread wider, from HB33 on January 5 to HB692 on April 13. A compressed filing window on one subject and a long tail on another suggests the data center bills moved as a group, while privacy arrived as individual members filed.

The practical consequence for anyone tracking Kentucky is that the bill list cannot distinguish a serious proposal from a message bill. Every entry here is a title and a date. The data holds no text, no sponsor, no committee assignment, no vote, and no outcome, so the count of six is a count of filings and nothing more.

How many Kentucky bills in 2026 mentioned data centers?
Five carry the exact title "AN ACT relating to data centers": HB593, HB856, HB544, SB319, and SB330. Two more, HB314 and SB64, address the Kentucky Communications Network Authority, which is a related but distinct subject.

Did any of these bills become law?
The data does not say. It contains bill numbers, titles, filing dates, and LegiScan links, with no status, vote, or enactment information.

What did HB455, the artificial intelligence bill, actually propose?
The data does not hold it. HB455 is listed only as "AN ACT relating to artificial intelligence and declaring an emergency," filed February 23, 2026, with no text or summary.

How many data privacy bills did Kentucky file in 2026?
Four: HB692, HB633, HB559, and HB33. HB559 adds "portability, and interoperability" to the standard data privacy title.

Is there any Kentucky bill about AI and power or electricity?
No bill title in the list mentions power, electricity, or utilities. The closest connection is indirect, through the data center bills and the two Communications Network Authority bills.

What does the one news item on the page cover?
It is dated September 14, 2026, and is headlined "Jobs AI Can't Easily Replace in Indiana and Kentucky." It is the only news item in the data and covers two states, not Kentucky alone.
